records.title: A Bi-level Co-design Framework for Lunar Monoped with 2D Jump and Landing Control
records.summary: Legged robots for lunar exploration must be designed for low gravity, where reduced contact forces and long flight phases make leg morphology and controller choice interdependent. We study this for a planar monoped in lunar gravity ($1.625$ m/s$^2$) using a bi-level co-design framework: a differential evolution outer loop searches over link lengths, and each candidate is evaluated on a vertical jump by either a quadratic program based task-space controller (QP-TSC) or a direct-collocation based trajectory optimization. The two controllers yield different optimal link lengths, and trajectory optimization outperforms the QP-TSC across most of the design space, with 17% lower Cost of Transport (COT) at their respective optima. We then extend to a 2D jump, where trajectory optimization with centroidal angular momentum regulation produces stable in-place and forward jumps, and an LQR controller absorbs impact and stabilizes the robot after touchdown. This is demonstrated on a baseline morphology with both links 0.3 m long.

records.title: A Data-Derived Scaling Approach for Plume-Surface Interaction Crater Formation
records.summary: This work presents a methodology for scaling test-scale plume-surface interaction (PSI) crater formation data to flight-scale. Methods for scaling both crater erosion rate and crater geometry (width and depth) were derived from scaling relationships proposed by previous PSI studies. Two methods for predicting crater width were investigated - one using an empirical scaling law for the crater aspect ratio and another informed by surface shear stress profiles from computational fluid dynamics (CFD). Data from three independent studies were then used to assess the performance of the developed scaling methodology. Results show that data from all three sources agree well with the crater erosion rate scaling methodology, with the caveat that limited data exist in regimes truly relevant to landing on the Moon. The performance of the geometry scaling methodology was more nuanced. The empirical scaling for crater aspect ratio performed well against PSI data obtained under Earth-atmospheric ambient pressure, but did a poor job of predicting the aspect ratio of craters formed from highly underexpanded plumes under vacuum conditions. Data from the Human Landing System (HLS) program’s Plume Surface Interaction Ground Test will be used to further improve the performance of the scaling methodology and to provide flight-scale predictions for PSI effects caused by HLS landers.
keywords: Lunar and Planetary Science and Exploration

records.title: A Missed Thrust Framework for Low-Thrust Spiral Trajectories to the NRHO
records.summary: A framework is developed by which end-to-end optimization of many-revolution low-thrust spiral trajectories can be completed in the presence of missed thrust events. This framework is applied to the Lunar Transit trajectory by which the initial capability of NASA’s Gateway lunar space station will be delivered to a Near Rectilinear Halo Orbit. This low-thrust mission consists of three subphases, each designed according to the specific objectives and dynamical regimes encountered as the mission progresses from a medium Earth insertion orbit to cislunar space. The presented framework accounts for the unique considerations demanded by each mission phase and incorporates appropriate capabilities into a novel mission analysis tool. This methodology enables large scale and reliable analyses of missed thrust events across the end-to-end Lunar Transit to verify the robustness of flight trajectories across the full range of considered launch dates.

records.title: A new model for cavitation in rocket engine turbopump inducers
records.summary: To enable exploration of the Moon and Mars, launch vehicles must be capable of throttled landing, which requires turbopump inducers to operate under more extreme conditions. Improved modeling that relies on fundamental physics as opposed to empirical formulation is therefore necessary to reliably accommodate this wider operating envelope. The goal of the proposed research is to improve CFD modeling of cavitation in turbopump inducers through a two-pronged approach: (1) improve the fundamental understanding of cavitation bubble growth so that computationally less-expensive models may operate without empirical coefficients and (2) estimate cavitation behavior in turbopump inducers at a large number of operating conditions based on only several CFD simulation results, extending the usefulness of computationally-expensive models. To achieve these goals the proposal (1) outlines a new model for cavitation bubble growth that differs from the conventional models implemented in CFD simulations, then (2) proposes how this new model may be used to estimate cavitating turbopump performance at new operating conditions from existing data or simulations. The proposal describes two experimental campaigns to verify and improve the model.

records.title: A Physics-Based Work-Energy Formulation for Real-Time Trajectory Guidance of a Lunar Lander
records.summary: Many sophisticated mathematical approaches have been developed to calculate and optimized trajectory solutions for lunar landing systems, including but not limited to Hamilton’s Principle of Variation, Pontryagin’s maximum principle, and convex optimization techniques among others. Many of these approaches require expensive computational resources in order to achieve convergence to a solution, which may be problematic due to the well known limitations in computational power and memory capacity of space hardened computers when compared to modern computers. In an effort to reduce complexity and the computational load required to generate the real-time guidance commands that are necessary during manual piloting, a simple physics-based work-energy approach is formulated. This approach is based on the dissipation of mechanical energy of the vehicle in reference to the final energy state required to achieve a safe landing. The rocket engine(s) used during landing and other maneuvers dissipate mechanical energy both by doing work against the velocity vector of the vehicle and by jettisoning mass. Therefore, by analytically solving the energy dissipation problem during every step of the maneuver, a much simpler algebraic solution that naturally and quickly attains convergence is obtained. This concept is not limited to approach and landing, but it may also be applied to de-orbiting, braking-burn, and divert maneuvers. The principle also applies for other type of maneuvers such as ascent and orbital insertion, where instead of energy dissipation, the engine injects the necessary energy into the system to attain the desired final state.
keywords: Lunar and Planetary Science and Exploration

records.title: A Reproducible Reconstruction and Evaluation Framework for Photorealistic Lunar Analog Scene Reconstruction Toward Digital Twins
records.summary: In this paper, we present a reconstruction pipeline that empirically quantifies the photorealistic scene reconstruction accuracy from both human-controlled and rover mast camera monocular feeds against physical ground truth as a function of Lunar traversal effects (e.g., motion blur, haze due to lofted regolith, trajectory bias, and sparse views). First, we benchmark six variants of 3D Gaussian Splatting (3DGS) across three Lunar analog scenes on held-out test sets using standard photometric metrics. We then establish how under traversal effects, this test-set-specific Novel View Synthesis (NVS) performance does not proportionally scale to the same photometric metrics in the reconstructed DTs. Our results quantify that splat training metrics alone are insufficient predictors of Cross-Reconstruction Photorealistic NVS Fidelity (CRPNVS), and that factors such as rover trajectory bias and geometric scene coverage play a critical role in determining the photorealistic quality of the reconstructed scenes targeting Lunar analog Digital Twins. Additionally, we pilot study Coverage Score ($S_c$), a geometry-based diagnostic derived from COLMAP poses and point cloud structure that provides a meaningful heuristic about the highest achievable CRPNVS structural fidelity, independently of splat training performance in the absence of a human-controlled reference. These findings establish a standardized, human control-referenced evaluation pipeline for photorealistic scene reconstruction for Lunar-analog Digital Twin development and future planetary exploration. Code and project page: https://rose-lab-admin.github.io/rose-lunar-dt-rec

records.title: A Systems Approach to Modeling Uncertain ODE Systems
records.summary: Incorporating the impacts of system uncertainty such as navigation errors, disturbance accelerations, burn execution biases and misalignments, orbit insertion dispersions, and a host of other influential factors into the design of a trajectory profile to make it robust to these unknown perturbations is becoming more feasible, particularly with the maturation of linear covariance analysis (LinCov) for closed-loop guidance, navigation, and control (GNC) systems. LinCov is an analytic technique for predicting stochastic behavior of dynamical systems. Previous studies interfaced a genetic algorithm (GA) with a linear covariance analysis tool to provide the initial demonstration of applying this non-traditional approach to robust trajectory optimization. These robust trajectory design techniques were originally developed for rendezvous applications in low Earth orbit. It was then extended to cis-lunar outbound trajectories to a Near Rectilinear Halo Orbit (NRHO) and introduced for a simple rendezvous approach trajectory in the NRHO for mid-course correction placement. Recently, these robust trajectory optimization principles have been applied to solve cislunar transfers to low-lunar orbit, NRHO rendezvous and docking, angles-only navigation for NRHO rendezvous, lunar powered descent and landing, along with Mars aerocapture problems. They were also utilized to determine the optimized trajectory correction burn placement for the upcoming Artemis II free-return cis-lunar trajectory profile and exercised to determine the optimized trajectory correction burn placement for NRHO orbit maintenance anticipated for the Artemis III mission. LinCov has also been used with a sweeping gradient method to perform robust optimal trajectory design for rendezvous in low-earth orbits and near rectilinear halo orbits. Recent developments in techniques generalize some of the modeling concepts and derive the corresponding governing equations. In this work, we present the software architecture for the Swift Integrated GNC and Mission Analysis (SIGMA) tool. In existing tools, the linear covariance analysis governing equations for particular models were implemented manually, involving significant development effort to derive and code partial derivatives and ensure proper bookkeeping for a variety of scenario configurations. SIGMA takes a different approach, modeling scenarios by connecting individual system models representing physical or GNC subsystems. By leveraging Condor for automatic differentiation and an engineering-focused modeling language, SIGMA is able to generate the functions required to perform covariance analysis. We have found that this reduces the number of configuration-specific special cases and reduces software development for performing analysis. The rest of the paper is organized as follows. records.title: Apollo 11 Lunar Module Touchdown Dynamics Reconstruction V and V for Human Landing Systems
records.summary: This paper presents an updated high-fidelity lunar landing dynamics simulation test bed developed at NASA Marshall Space Flight Center (MSFC) in support of the Human Landing System (HLS) program, with verification support from NASA Langley Research Center (LaRC). The MSFC GeneraLized Aerospace Simulation in Simulink® (GLASS) program uses MATLAB®/Simulink® and Simscape™ Multibody™ to model detailed contact dynamics of lunar regolith, shock absorbers, footpads, and multibody linkages, laying the groundwork for integrated analyses incorporating in-the-loop guidance, navigation, and control systems. For validation, the simulation focuses on pure landing dynamics and is benchmarked against Apollo 11 flight data and independent modern reconstructions. The GLASS simulation demonstrates excellent agreement with historical Apollo data, validating the approach against real-world landing dynamics. Further, strong correlation between the MSFC and LaRC simulation results across different platforms provides verification of the modeling methodology. This collaborative effort establishes confidence in the simulation framework and provides a solid foundation for comprehensive HLS system analysis. The paper details the modeling methodology, validation against Apollo data, and verification through comparison with Zupp’s reconstruction and LaRC’s MSC Automated Dynamic Analysis of Mechanical Systems (Adams) reconstruction results.

records.title: Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle as Traversed Performance Metrics: Preparing for Artemis Mobile Vehicle Traverse Planning
records.summary: Introduction: Having mobile assets as part of a planetary exploration mission has proven to significantly increase the scientific return of a mission as evidenced by the Apollo Lunar Roving Vehicle (LRV) and the numerous Mars rovers. This abstract focuses on the characterization of the as-traversed lunar terrain and performance demonstrated of the LRV to inform future traverse planning for Artemis vehicles. This abstract quantifies the speed made good (SMG) for the Apollo 15 and 16 LRV EVAs and compares that to the slope and detrended terrain ruggedness of the landing sites and exploration area experienced along each traverse path. The LRVs were designed to navigate a 20 – 23° slope in “favorable conditions” with a max of 25°. The LRV could theoretically achieve speeds of 9 – 13 km/hr (2.5 – 3.6 m/s). Having these Apollo as demonstrated traverse metrics will be a useful starting point to understand how mobility assets will perform at the lunar south pole. Methods: SMG was calculated to understand the actual average speed achieved during individual traverses. These values were compared to the average slope and terrain ruggedness for each traverse to explore any potential correlations between SMG and surface characteristics. To quantify the SMG of the Apollo traverses, start/stop times were pulled from the transcripts that are part of the Apollo lunar surface journals [1]. The duration it took to drive between stations is then divided by the actual traverse distance quantified using the vector files provided by the Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter Camera (LROC) team. Slope and detrended terrain ruggedness index were calculated using the 2 mpp NAC DTM. Results: The surface characteristics analyzed, and SMG calculated for Apollo 15 and 16 EVAs are summarized in Table 1 and plotted in Figures 1 and 2. Discussion: Overall, the results show that the Apollo 15 and 16 LRVs performed within or near the expected capabilities. The average slope of each traverse was well within the expected limits of LRV capabilities, and the max slopes did not exceed the capabilities. The as-traversed speeds were, on average, lower than expected. However, there are times in the transcripts where the astronauts noted higher speeds than what is evident in the SMG calculations. The Apollo 16 mission report states the LRV achieved speeds up to 14 km/hr (3.8 m/s) [1]. There are several variables that could have contributed to the average LRV speeds being less than the design specifications including the astronauts learning how to operate the LRV on the surface, mechanical problems (the Apollo 15 LRV front steering mechanism was non-functional), and more cautious driving adapted to the physical surface environment. However, comparisons of SMG to the average slope and TRI did not result in any strong correlations. records.title: Artemis I Space Launch System Base Heat Shield Thermal Protection System Performance
records.summary: The Space Launch System (SLS) Core Stage base heat shield experienced the highest external heating environments on the entire launch vehicle during Artemis I ascent flight. This result was consistent with design predictions. The base heat shield experiences P50 cork combustion dynamics at low altitudes, plume-induced recirculation at moderate altitudes and then in-space base flow physics out to Main Engine Cut-Off (MECO). The base heat shield thermal protection system (TPS) is composed of a P50 cork ablator which is bonded to a substrate. The heat shield protects the gimbal actuation system, RS-25 turbomachinery systems and other aft section sensitive components during ascent. This paper estimates the base heat shield TPS performance from Artemis I using flight data from the NASA Langley Research Center’s Scientifically Calibrated In-Flight Imagery (SCIFLI) Airborne Multispectral Imager (SAMI), development flight instrumentation (DFI) and other TPS recession flight measurements. Predictions from computational and ground test-derived engineering ablation models and observations are also applied. Since no base heat shield substrate thermocouple data were obtained for Artemis I, an estimate of the TPS performance data is derived here. This data assesses thermal margin of the SLS Core Stage base heat shield and best informs the Artemis II Crewed mission to the moon.

records.title: Artemis II Descent and Landing: A Preliminary Performance Assessment of the Orion Parachute System
records.summary: The Artemis II mission, which sent four NASA astronauts to the vicinity of the Moon for the first time in over 50 years, ended with a safe touchdown in the Pacific Ocean courtesy of a series of 11 parachutes. An initial assessment of the Orion parachute system during the mission can be performed with preliminary air-to-air imagery captured during the descent and landing. Due to both planned and unplanned nonrecovery of jettisoned parachute hardware, as well as the absence of individual riser load measurements, analysis will rely heavily on high-resolution imagery. Interrogation of this imagery can provide insight into not only parachute performance, but also into important Entry, Descent, and Landing (EDL) triggers and actions. While the terminal performance of the system appears nominal and consistent with previous drop test and missions, anomalies related to vehicle debris liberation and parachute reefing are apparent.

records.title: Artemis II Translunar Injection Aborts Trajectory Design and Optimization
records.summary: The Artemis II translunar injection (TLI) abort architecture defines contingency trajectories and operational procedures to ensure crew safety during the critical maneuver that transitions Orion from Earth orbit onto a lunar bound trajectory. Off-nominal performance, subsystem anomalies, or loss of communication can place the crew in dynamically sensitive regimes that require well-characterized abort options, including but not limited to, early return opportunities, abort initiation time of ignition (TIG) strategies and engine selection tradeoffs. This work presents launch period analyses, trajectory class delineations and implementation trade studies for both highly elliptical orbit (HEO) and translunar orbit abort families, using large scale automation sweeps and high-fidelity optimization to provide comprehensive coverage of the abort design space.

records.title: Artemis III Site Selection Update: Downselection From Thirteen to Nine Candidate Regions
records.summary: Introduction: In 2022 the National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) publicly announced the 13 candidate Artemis III regions. These locations, near the Moon’s south pole, will host the Agency’s first crewed mission back to the lunar surface in over 50 years [1]. Since then, the Artemis III site-selection effort has continued to mature through additional analysis and refinement of constraints. In October 2024 at the Lunar Exploration Analysis Group (LEAG) meeting at Johnson Space Center, NASA announced an updated set of nine candidate Artemis III landing regions which have been refined from the original 13 [2]. This abstract provides an update to the initial 2022 announcement , documenting the status of the effort. to refine the candidate list and summarizing key considerations which informed the selection. Updated Candidate Regions: Shown in Image 1 is the updated set of Artemis III candidate landing regions – Peak near Cabeus B, Haworth, Malapert Massif, Mons Mouton Plateau, Mons Mouton, Nobile Rim 1, Nobile Rim 2, de Gerlache Rim 2, and Slater Plain. They represent the outcome of more than two years of continued assessment since the original announcement in 2022. Each region includes multiple landing sites and provides flexibility for further site-specific evaluation. Analysis Process: During this period, Artemis III mission assumptions evolved, including updates to vehicle performance and trajectory analyses based on the SpaceX human Landing System (HLS) design. Mission-level assessments increasingly emphasized end-to-end mission availability, capturing the combined effects of launch opportunities, transit and rendezvous geometry, communication constraints, landing performance, surface illumination, and terrain safety. These constraints are evaluated simultaneously on a calendar basis, reflecting the operational realties of a crewed lunar mission. Artemis III in-space operations will be conducted from a Near-Rectilinear Halo Orbit (NRHO), which provides favorable Earth visibility and access to the south pole region but imposes strong temporal and geometric constraints on surface access. Surface stay duration varies approximately 5.75 to 6.25 days depending on mission epoch plus low lunar orbit rev considerations, resulting in time-dependent accessibility that differs by region. As analyses matured, regions demonstrating greater robustness across mission epochs and reduced sensitivity to seasonal effects were favored. Terrain safety remains a primary consideration, with assessments focused on minimizing the degree of slope variability within a landing ellipse, consistent with various aspects of the integrated architecture. Regions that maintain sufficient low-slope area to accommodate a safe landing were prioritized. In parallel, candidate regions were evaluated for the presence and distribution of hazardous surface features, including impact craters, block populations, and rough or highly variable terrain that could pose risk during ...

records.title: Autonomous Trajectory Anomaly Detection and Replanning in Cislunar Space
records.summary: Future NASA missions in cislunar space and beyond will require increased onboard autonomy to ensure safety, resilience, and affordability. Current operations rely heavily on ground-based teams and the Deep Space Network (DSN) to monitor trajectories and correct deviations -- an approach that is becoming unsustainable as mission volume grows through programs such as Artemis, Gateway, and expanded robotic exploration. Limited communications availability and increasing delays pose particular risks for crewed and deep-space missions, where rapid response to unexpected events may be required without timely Earth contact. This proposal addresses this challenge by developing and testing a new onboard capability for autonomous trajectory detection, corrective maneuvering, and trajectory replanning in the cislunar environment. The goal of this research is to develop and test a new approach to detect trajectory anomalies and respond using current mission constraints and spacecraft capabilities to inform maneuvers or replanning. This goal will be achieved by the following objectives: 1) adapt an isolation-based methodology for detecting anomalous trajectories to spacecraft motion of various geometries and sensitivity in cislunar space; 2) formulate adaptive anomaly maneuver responses and implement a post-execution verification system to detect and correct action anomalies; 3) develop an autonomous trajectory replanning method to reach the desired final state based on current system constraints and ensuring navigational efficiency; and 4) perform processor-in-the-loop testing to validate real-time operability and performance on spacecraft-representative hardware. By moving these activities onboard, the work aims to reduce reliance on the DSN, improve mission robustness during critical phases, and enable lower-cost missions with greater operational flexibility. To accomplish these objectives, the research combines isolation-based anomaly detection with motion-primitive-based trajectory planning. A compact onboard database of representative spacecraft motions will be constructed using motion primitives that capture typical expected trajectories of the mission. Real-time spacecraft motion will be compared against this database to compute an anomaly score, enabling early detection of unexpected behavior in the sensitive multi-body environment near the Moon. records.title: Birkhoff conjecture and finite energy foliations in Hill's lunar problem
records.summary: We prove Birkhoff's retrograde orbit conjecture in Hill's lunar problem by showing that the retrograde orbit bounds a disk-like global surface of section for every energy below the critical value. We also obtain a global description of the dynamics through the critical energy level by constructing finite energy foliations for energies slightly above it. The binding of these foliations consists of the retrograde orbit together with the Lyapunov orbits near the critical points. As a consequence, there exist infinitely many periodic orbits and infinitely many trajectories asymptotic to the Lyapunov orbits. The proof combines pseudo-holomorphic curve techniques with a new convexity theorem for Hill's lunar problem. More precisely, we construct an explicit global symplectic change of coordinates under which the bounded regularized component becomes strictly convex up to the critical energy level. This convexity implies strong dynamical consequences, including lower bounds for the Conley-Zehnder indices of periodic orbits, and allows the application of the Hofer-Wysocki-Zehnder theory of finite energy foliations. As a result, we obtain disk-like global surfaces of section below the critical level and $2-3-2$ foliations for energies slightly above it.

records.title: Can Julia land on the Moon? On the development of a GNC simulation framework for the Argonaut lunar lander
records.summary: No, the Julia programming language cannot land on the Moon - but it can play a crucial role in designing and analysing the Guidance, Navigation, and Control (GNC) algorithms required for doing so. This paper presents the development of a lunar landing simulation framework implemented in Julia at the European Space Agency (ESA), within the Argonaut lunar lander programme. ATLAS (Argonaut Tools for Landing Analysis and Simulation) is a modular suite of analysis and simulation tools that cover the complete descent and landing phase of Argonaut, integrating high fidelity translational and rotational dynamics, varying mass properties, propellant sloshing, detailed sensor and actuator models, and flight-representative GNC algorithms within a multi-rate simulation environment. The framework is intended to bridge early-phase prototyping and large-scale Monte Carlo analysis within a single environment. This work evaluates the advantages and limitations of adopting Julia compared to established GNC development practices based on the MATLAB/Simulink ecosystem. The results show that Julia provides a powerful, flexible, and high-performance environment for agency-driven research, early-phase design studies, and computationally intensive closed-loop simulations enabling large-scale, parallelizable simulations and rapid design iteration cycles.

records.title: Chang'e 7 Lunar Lander Optical Camera-Telescope: Optical Astronomy from the Moon
records.summary: We report the design and manufacture of a new, lightweight, wide-field, optical camera-telescope on board the Chang'e 7 lunar mission (launched in August 2026 and due for lunar touchdown in late November 2026). The camera is capable of static, panchromatic imagery within a $420-696~nm$ optical wavelength range. The camera was designed and built under the small lunar astronomy observation station program of the Chinese National Space Agency (CNSA) as a collaboration between the International Lunar Observatory Association of Hawaii (ILOA), the Laboratory for Space Research (LSR) of the University of Hong Kong (HKU) and the Beijing Institute of Space Mechanics and Electricity (BISME). The camera has been built to meet science goals of the mission for sustainable astronomical operation over a large range of temperatures from the Moon's south pole. We report on the design and ground based preliminary performance, together with an analysis of the camera's simulated output to indicate the range of astronomical observations possible from the lunar surface given the camera's limited sensitivity and angular resolution given the modest aperture and wide field of view.

records.title: Chang'e-6 lander reveals local hour-scale temporal variations in lunar surface water
records.summary: Lunar surface water primarily originates from solar wind irradiation, with diurnal variations in its content observed by orbital and ground-based remote sensing. However, low temporal resolution and the lack of accurate in-situ surface observations have limited understanding of the magnitude of these variations. Here, we report analysis results of the in-situ infrared spectra at the same location across different local times acquired by the Chang'e-6 lander. The in-situ spectra were calibrated for thermal contributions based on laboratory measurements conducted on the returned lunar soils, showing clear OH/H 2 O absorption signals. The OH/H 2 O contents achieved from the in-situ spectra exhibit significant temporal variations, with a notable decrease of 37%-58% from ∼10:00 a.m. to ∼11:03 a.m. local time. The discovery confirms not only the diurnal water variations detected by remote sensing but also extends such variations to the hourly range. The OH/H 2 O content decreasing rate is ∼8.4 ± 0.4 ppm/K in the high temperature range (349-358 K), faster than in the low temperature period (∼5.5 ppm/K for 309 K to 319 K). This indicates that temperature exerts a dominant control on the variation of OH/H 2 O content. Hydrogen exists in various forms in lunar soil grains and solar wind flux over a lunar day is insufficient to replenish the depleted OH/H 2 O. Therefore, the occurrence of OH/H 2 O, the only form detectable by infrared spectroscopy, is highly temperature dependent. The new discoveries shed light on the distribution and recycling of water on the lunar surface.

records.title: Chang'E-6 reveals solar wind-dependent H- ions on the Moon
records.summary: Apart from positive ions and electrons, negative ions are expected in various astrophysical environments. However, they have never been detected on the Moon until the Chang'E-6 mission. The NILS instrument onboard Chang'E-6 lander is the first dedicated instrument for detecting negative ions beyond Earth and has successfully obtained H - spectra on the lunar surface, providing an unprecedented opportunity to investigate their origin and distribution. Here, we present a positive correlation between the H - spectra and solar wind parameters, which provides direct evidence for the generation of negative ions from solar wind-surface interaction. Combined with Monte Carlo simulations, we predict a thin dayside H - layer and a long nightside H - tail, which can contribute to the lunar plasma environment, especially during an extreme solar wind density event. These findings greatly improve our understanding of the generation and distribution of negative ions on the Moon and other airless bodies.
