records.title: Data Mining-Based Cislunar Escape-Family Analysis in The Multi-Body Models
records.summary: Escape trajectories from the Earth-Moon system play an important role in interplanetary transfer. This paper focuses on the escape trajectories from a 167 km circular Earth orbit in the Earth-Moon planar circular three-body problem and the Sun-Earth/Moon planar bicircular four-body problem and is denoted to providing a comprehensive analysis on these escape trajectories. To achieve these purposes, the global maps of escape trajectories are constructed, and escape trajectories with one lunar gravity assist are pre-filtered. Then, an effective method to identification escape families is proposed based on dynamical analysis and data mining techniques. Once the escape families are identified, the corresponding characteristics are analyzed to provide insights into the construction of escape trajectories. Based on these escape families, the effects of the solar gravity perturbation on the number of escape trajectories, the emergence and disappearance of escape families, variation in generalized energy, and transfer characteristics are further summarized, providing insights into the model selection in the escape trajectory construction. This paper establishes an analysis methodology of escape trajectories from a perspective of escape families, deepening the understanding of escape dynamics.

records.title: Data-Driven Terramechanics Approach Towards a Realistic Real-Time Simulator for Lunar Rovers
records.summary: High-fidelity simulators for the lunar surface provide a digital environment for extensive testing of rover operations and mission planning. However, current simulators focus on either visual realism or physical accuracy, which limits their capability to replicate lunar conditions comprehensively. This work addresses that gap by combining high visual fidelity with realistic terrain interaction for a realistic representation of rovers on the lunar surface. Because direct simulation of wheel-soil interactions is computationally expensive, a data-driven approach was adopted, using regression models for slip and sinkage from data collected in both full-rover and single-wheel experiments and simulations. The resulting regression-based terramechanics model accurately reproduced steady-state and dynamic slip, as well as sinkage behavior, on flat terrain and slopes up to 20 degrees, with validation against field test results. Additionally, improvements were made to enhance the realism of terrain deformation and wheel trace visualization. This method supports real-time applications that require physically plausible terrain response alongside high visual fidelity.

records.title: Decoupled Thrust-Axis Attitude Control Using Quaternions for Chandrayaan-3 Lunar Landing Mission
records.summary: Chandrayaan-3 mission achieved a historic milestone with its successful soft landing near the lunar south pole, highlighting the critical role of the navigation, guidance, and control (NGC) system. Navigation provided vehicle state estimates relative to the Moon center, while a polynomial based guidance scheme computed the required acceleration profile to meet terminal landing conditions. This acceleration demand was translated into total thrust magnitude and attitude commands generation. Attitude command generation involved aligning the thrust axis with the required acceleration vector and constraining rotation about the thrust axis, typically governed by mission-specific requirements. Although quaternion-based control laws are preferred for their singularity-free representation, they inherently couple all three rotational axes. This coupling can lead to undesirable interactions between guidance and control, especially during large rotations about the thrust axis, due to the quaternion shortest-path property. This paper proposes a novel quaternion-based decoupling method that enables independent thrust-axis control, mitigating guidance-control interaction and ensuring proper attitude commands generation for lander attitude control.

records.title: Demonstrating the Priority of Lunar Orbital Port Over Lunar Surface Construction: A Descent Corridor with Electromagnetic Cargo Reception
records.summary: Abstract Plans for lunar development, including the Artemis and International Lunar Research Station plans, assume that bases are built on the lunar surface.1,2 Yet landing is both energy-intensive and failure-prone: only about half of the soft-landing attempts made since 1966 have fully succeeded,3–7 and the surface exposes crews and equipment to long-lasting moonquakes, radiation and sharp-edged dust.8–15 Here we show that long-term stationing, production and logistics are better placed in low lunar orbit, in a distributed ‘Lunar Orbital Port’, than on the surface. Orbital-mechanics calculations indicate that holding a frozen lunar orbit costs propellant comparable to or lower than reboosting the International Space Station,16 whereas landing and departing demands several km/s of velocity change.17,18We then describe a descent corridor in which cargo ejected from the port in a spindle-shaped capsule is decelerated by a long electromagnetic track on the lunar surface, which returns most of the kinetic energy as electricity. This concept study suggests that the main construction layer of lunar development can be placed in orbit first and the surface settled afterwards, and that the delivery corridor is the key technology to verify first.

records.title: Design and Experimental Validation of the Separation and Deployment System for the CHERI Lunar Micro-Rovers
records.summary: Reliable separation mechanisms are critical for planetary micro-rovers, which must withstand launch vibrations and then eject the vehicle clear of the lander. This paper presents the design, optimization, and testing of the separation system of the CHERI (Challenging Environment Exploration Rovers for Intelligence) lunar micro-rovers. Sized for a 5 kg vehicle, the assembly comprises an aluminum ground plate, a central non-explosive hold-down and release mechanism, and an asymmetric four-spring ejection array. Initial separation trials revealed a velocity deficit caused by energy absorption in the flexible wheel-legs and chassis during the ejection stroke. This loss was represented as equivalent chassis damping in a multi-body dynamic model, and the springs were re-optimized accordingly. Early hardware iterations failed vibration testing, first through spring jamming in the guide housings and then through a 34 Hz fundamental mode of the flat ground plate. A density-based topology optimization raised the fundamental frequency to 84 Hz, above the 70 Hz requirement of the lander, within a 1.6 kg mass budget. The final configuration passed acceptance-level sinusoidal vibration, random vibration, and shock testing without structural degradation. Separation tests with a weight-matched one-sixth mass model, tracked by optical motion capture, confirmed clearance of the lander and reproduced the simulated free flight to within the run-to-run variation of the measured ejection velocity. These tests further showed that landing outcome is dominated by touchdown and settling dynamics, indicating that the residual pitch rate is the main controllable design parameter and confirming self-righting recovery as an integral element of the deployment architecture.

records.title: Design and implementation of thermal control strategy for micro-size lunar exploration rover hakuto
records.summary: The research focuses on the thermal interface design of the HAKUTO Rover Flight Model (FM) and its evaluation using the final thermal vacuum experiment. Initially, an analytical thermal model was developed, dividing the rover into six distinct radiating surfaces. The surface temperature of the rover was then determined based on its orientation relative to the solar radiative flux, as well as other thermal factors such as lunar radiation, solar albedo, and conduction from the lunar regolith. By considering the impact of these heat sources, suitable mounting locations for the avionics and the angle of the solar panels were determined to optimize the rover's thermal performance and power generation while ensuring the rover's mass remained under 4 kg. After the preliminary thermal analysis, numerical computational simulations were conducted to further elaborate on the thermal response of the final HAKUTO Rover FM design, which was then verified through a thermal balance test in a vacuum environment.

records.title: Design of Lunar Soil Simulant for Lunar Landing Applications and Its Mechanical Property Evolution under Impact Loading
records.summary: Abstract There is a critical shortage of lunar soil simulants (LSS) tailored for the far side of the Moon and the South Pole, and the evolution of lunar soil mechanical properties under realistic lander footpad impact conditions remains poorly understood, especially the response laws under different landing slopes. In this study, a dedicated LSS for landing impact tests was developed using Changbai Mountain volcanic ash as the base material, based on lunar soil characteristics from the far side and South Pole-Aitken (SPA) basin. The LSS was prepared through crushing, grinding, sieving and gradation optimization, and a 10 m×10 m test bed was constructed. Impact simulation tests were performed using a four-legged lander on four typical slopes (0°, 4°, 8°, 12°). Combined with direct shear and consolidation compression tests, the spatial evolution of shear strength and compression properties of the LSS after impact was analyzed. The results show that the particle size distribution of the volcanic ash-based LSS falls within the range of natural lunar soil and matches the gradation trend of Chang'e-5 samples. Key mechanical parameters (dry density, cohesion, internal friction angle) agree well with those of Apollo and Chang'e real lunar soils. Landing slope significantly affects the spatial distribution of post-impact mechanical properties: shear strength weakens on the uphill side and strengthens on the downhill side, while void ratio shows the opposite gradient. This distribution pattern stabilizes when the slope exceeds 8°. The findings provide important experimental basis for lunar soil mechanical evaluation, lander stability analysis and ground verification of future lunar exploration missions.

records.title: Designing 3D transfers: application to Earth-Moon
records.summary: Three dimensional Earth-Moon transfers usually consume more fuel than planar ones, but are needed depending on the latitude of the launch site and the desired inclination of the final lunar orbit. A systematic search of the optimal 3D transfers represents a true challenge due the dimension of the parameter set to span. In this paper, we propose a new method to design 3D transfers using a tangential velocity constraint for the burns, modeled using the overdetermined constraints technique based on the Theory of Functional Connections for an optimal search of solutions in a numerically efficient way. The developed method is applied here for a systematic study of optimal 3D Earth-Moon transfers, but could be used to design any type of 3D maneuvers.

records.title: DrEAM Deliveries and SCIFLI Reentry Data Mark Key Milestones for Dragonfly and Artemis II
records.summary: Recent progress in NASA’s Dragonfly and Artemis programs marks two major milestones in entry, descent, and landing research. Most Dragonfly Entry Aerosciences Measurements (DrEAM) sensors have been delivered to Lockheed Martin Space for integration, enabling a comprehensive in‑situ dataset of Titan’s upper-atmosphere and vehicle aerothermal performance. Together with the German Aerospace Center’s Data Acquisition System, these instruments support validation of thermal protection and aerodynamic models ahead of Dragonfly’s planned 2028 launch. Concurrently, NASA’s SCIFLI team successfully captured multispectral airborne imagery during the Artemis II crew module’s high‑speed reentry, providing critical real‑world heating observations that refine superorbital reentry predictions. Post‑flight assessments of Orion confirm improved heat‑shield behavior, effective launch‑pad enhancements, and successful recovery operations, strengthening confidence in the architecture and schedule for Artemis III and future lunar surface missions.

records.title: Dual-Horizon Hybrid Internal Model for Low-Gravity Quadrupedal Jumping with Hardware-in-the-Loop Validation
records.summary: Locomotion under reduced gravity is commonly realized through jumping, yet continuous pronking in lunar gravity remains challenging due to prolonged flight phases and sparse ground contact. The extended aerial duration increases landing impact sensitivity and makes stable attitude regulation over rough planetary terrain difficult. Existing approaches primarily address single jumps on flat surfaces and lack both continuous-terrain solutions and realistic hardware validation. This work presents a Dual-Horizon Hybrid Internal Model for continuous quadrupedal jumping under lunar gravity using proprioceptive sensing only. Two temporal encoders capture complementary time scales: a short-horizon branch models rapid vertical dynamics with explicit vertical velocity estimation, while a long-horizon branch models horizontal motion trends and center-of-mass height evolution across the jump cycle. The fused representation enables stable and continuous jumping under extended aerial phases characteristic of lunar gravity. To provide hardware-in-the-loop validation, we develop the MATRIX (Mixed-reality Adaptive Testbed for Robotic Integrated eXploration) platform, a digital-twin-driven system that offloads gravity through a pulley-counterweight mechanism and maps Unreal Engine lunar terrain to a motion platform and treadmill in real time. Using MATRIX, we demonstrate continuous jumping of a quadruped robot under lunar-gravity emulation across cratered lunar-like terrain.

records.title: Dynamic Modeling and Attitude Control of a Reaction-Wheel-Based Low-Gravity Bipedal Hopper
records.summary: Planetary bodies characterized by low gravitational acceleration, such as the Moon and near-Earth asteroids, impose unique locomotion constraints due to diminished contact forces and extended airborne intervals. Among traversal strategies, hopping locomotion offers high energy efficiency but is prone to mid-flight attitude instability caused by asymmetric thrust generation and uneven terrain interactions. This paper presents an underactuated bipedal hopping robot that employs an internal reaction wheel to regulate body posture during the ballistic flight phase. The system is modeled as a gyrostat, enabling analysis of the dynamic coupling between torso rotation and reaction wheel momentum. The locomotion cycle comprises three phases: a leg-driven propulsive jump, mid-air attitude stabilization via an active momentum exchange controller, and a shock-absorbing landing. A reduced-order model is developed to capture the critical coupling between torso rotation and reaction wheel dynamics. The proposed framework is evaluated in MuJoCo-based simulations under lunar gravity conditions (g = 1.625 m/s^2). Results demonstrate that activation of the reaction wheel controller reduces peak mid-air angular deviation by more than 65% and constrains landing attitude error to within 3.5 degrees at touchdown. Additionally, actuator saturation per hop cycle is reduced, ensuring sufficient control authority. Overall, the approach significantly mitigates in-flight attitude excursions and enables consistent upright landings, providing a practical and control-efficient solution for locomotion on irregular extraterrestrial terrains.

records.title: Effective Stability of Near-Rectilinear Halo Orbits in the Earth-Moon System
records.summary: Near-rectilinear halo orbits (NRHOs) around Earth-Moon L2 in the Circular Restricted 3-Body Problem (CR3BP) exhibit a complex dynamical landscape, featuring a band of normally elliptic orbits embedded within regions of strong instability. This coexistence of stable and unstable dynamics, amplified by the numerical sensitivity associated with close lunar passages, makes the long-term behavior of trajectories near NRHOs a delicate and intrinsically nonlinear problem. Understanding the effective stability of these elliptic orbits is therefore a critical challenge, lying at the intersection of local normal form theory and global instability mechanisms. To quantify finite-time confinement, we formulate a rigorous framework for effective stability using discrete Poincaré maps. By employing jet transport to compute high-order Taylor expansions, we construct explicit polynomial normal forms. We derive discrete Nekhoroshev-type estimates by identifying the normalization order, which balances the asymptotic convergence of the map's analyticity domain against the cumulative penalty of low-order small divisors. Applying this framework to the Earth-Moon system, we map the resulting geometric limits directly into physical spatial coordinates. Crucially, we demonstrate that for practical mission lifetimes (e.g., 10-50 years), the required stability is vastly shorter than the characteristic Nekhoroshev accumulation time. Consequently, the effective stability region is not constrained by the time-dependent exponential drift, but is instead governed entirely by the maximum analytical domain of the optimized normal form. These derived spatial envelopes establish explicit geometric boundaries for the intrinsic local stability of elliptic NRHOs, providing a rigorous mathematical characterization of their nonlinear confinement within the CR3BP.

records.title: Embedded Normal Form Algorithms for Low-Cost Cislunar Navigation
records.summary: NASA and international partners are pushing the boundaries of space exploration, increasingly sending missions to complex dynamical environments such as cislunar space and multi-body Jovian systems. This growing complexity, especially with sustained programs like ARTEMIS, necessitates a shift away from simplified models that only consider one or two massive bodies. For decades, trajectory designers have used semi-analytical techniques to understand these environments. However, these techniques typically rely on truncated models that omit complex gravitational perturbations. These unmodeled forces lead to significant trajectory deviations over time, requiring frequent and costly correction maneuvers. I am proposing a method to apply semi-analytical techniques within higher-fidelity models. This approach captures the higher-order interactions and quasi-periodic forcing that define the true orbital environment. By doing so, we gain the analytical insight of traditional methods while providing a framework compatible with high-fidelity mission design. This allows us to map the gravitational scaffolding of a system with high precision and identify natural pathways that are often obscured in simpler models. The methodology involves developing a Quasi-Hill Restricted Four-Body Problem (QHR4BP) toolkit utilizing high-order normal form expansions. This enables the analytical classification of spacecraft motion to determine transit or stable orbit behavior without the iterative numerical integration that typically exhausts onboard processing power. The framework will be developed in Julia to leverage its specialized package ecosystem and ease of rapid development. For flight deployment, these algorithms will be translated into C++ or Rust to align with NASA flight software standards. The research concludes with Hardware-in-the-Loop (HIL) testing on microcontrollers to benchmark performance in simulated real-time scenarios. This proposal focuses on creating lightweight firmware-ready software optimized for low-SWaP (Size, Weight, and Power) edge computing hardware. Current high-fidelity navigation often requires computationally heavy algorithms that exceed the limits of radiation-hardened flight hardware. My research addresses this by providing near-instantaneous classification of motion. This enables autonomous maneuvering while using significantly less memory than ...

records.title: Enhancing Lunar PNT Performance Through Surface Station Enabled Radiometric Observables
records.summary: Future lunar surface missions require reliable positioning for autonomous rover operations. Lunar navigation satellite systems may provide limited vertical positioning accuracy due to satellite availability and observation geometry, particularly during early deployment. This study investigates a radiometric navigation architecture in which a lunar surface station (SS) improves rover positioning through double-differenced satellite observations and additional surface-to-surface ranging. Pseudorange and Doppler measurements from lunar navigation satellites are used for relative positioning between the SS and rover, while dual one-way ranging (DOWR) provides an additional range observable. The radiometric solution is integrated with rover dead-reckoning information. Monte Carlo simulations were conducted using five satellites representative of NASA's Lunar Communications Relay and Navigation Systems (LCRNS) constellation and a rover trajectory near Connecting Ridge at the lunar south pole. The results show that the SS improves horizontal and vertical relative positioning, with further gains from DOWR. In the simulated scenario, the mean 99.7% vertical positioning error decreased from 29.9 m without the SS to 5.5 m with double-differenced pseudorange and Doppler processing, and to 4.8 m with DOWR. An uncorrected DOWR hardware bias significantly degraded positioning, whereas the proposed bias-estimation method achieved a final estimation error of 0.058 +/- 0.057 m. The benefit of DOWR also depended on observation geometry. These results demonstrate the potential of a lunar surface station to improve vertical relative positioning through direct radiometric ranging, complementing its communication and navigation support roles.

records.title: Evaluation of Front-End Feature Matching for Lunar Visual SLAM
records.summary: Lunar rovers will primarily rely on cameras for localization until navigation satellite services are deployed, and will continue to need them afterwards for relative navigation, hazard detection, and surface operations. Visual odometry (VO) and Simultaneous Localization and Mapping (SLAM) mostly estimate motion by matching features between frames. However, feature matchers are developed on urban, indoor and driving scenes, planetary studies compare them on orbital registration or within complete SLAM systems, and real lunar imagery with reference poses is scarce, so matching between rover frames on low-texture, harshly lit terrain, and its effect on VO, has not been compared. We benchmark eleven classical and learned detector-matcher combinations on nine synthetic, lunar-testbed, and terrestrial-analogue datasets, and a feature tracker, scoring pairwise pose accuracy against baseline and the trajectory error of the resulting VO. Under a common rotation-only metric, the SuperPoint pairings outperform SIFT with ratio-tested FLANN matching on both lunar testbeds and one analogue site, with smaller or unresolved differences on synthetic data. When rotation and translation direction are scored jointly, this SIFT pairing exceeds both SuperPoint pairings on four synthetic datasets, so synthetic results alone do not establish relative performance on real rover imagery. In stereo VO, the SuperPoint pairings are not consistently more accurate than SIFT, but only they keep tracking on all eight sequential datasets. Pairings with classical detectors depend on lighting while SuperPoint changes little: a low spotlight makes them more accurate than diffuse light on the same testbed views, consistent with more contrast and detected keypoints. SuperPoint with LightGlue is the fastest learned combination (16 ms per frame), and DINOv2 retrieval proposals still need geometric verification.

records.title: Extravehicular Activity and Human Surface Mobility Program (EHP): Integrated Concept of Operations (ConOps)
records.summary: This Extravehicular Activity and Human Surface Mobility Program (EHP) Concept of Operations (ConOps) document captures a high-level definition of the prospective concepts of operations, capabilities, and operational interfaces across the current National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) exploration mission architecture options reflecting stakeholder expectations. EHP operations involve conducting Extravehicular Activities (EVAs) using the Exploration EVA (xEVA) System in both microgravity environments (such as cis-lunar space aboard Gateway) and partial gravity on the lunar surface. These operations also include traversing the lunar terrain using both the unpressurized Lunar Terrain Vehicle (LTV) and the Pressurized Rover (PR). Science activities conducted on these rovers will be opportunistic—meaning they will be supported by basic onboard capabilities, with scientific tasks designed to fit within the vehicles' operational parameters. EHP operations also encompass activities involving a secondary habitable volume, such as the Initial Surface Habitat (ISH), expected to be the Multi-Purpose Habitat (MPH), as well as interactions with the Lunar Surface Cargo Lander. Operations with other pre-formulation projects, will be included in upcoming revisions of this document as will operations during transit to Mars and Mars surface .

records.title: Faster Thermal Profiling of a Lunar Rover with Machine Learning Adapted Finite Difference Model
records.summary: Autonomous space systems operating in extreme thermal environments require accurate and efficient thermal modeling to support both pre-mission system design and onboard autonomy. For lunar rovers, large temperature gradients, radiative heat transfer, and variable surface conditions make reliable thermal prediction especially challenging. High-fidelity physics-based simulations provide accurate results but are computationally expensive, while simplified models and lookup-table approach often lack sufficient accuracy. Physics-informed machine learning (PIML) offers a promising alternative by combining data-driven models with embedded physical knowledge. This paper presents a PIML framework for thermal analysis of a simplified lunar rover with internal heat sources, where machine learning enables environment-adaptive coarse meshing. The proposed architecture integrates a transfer neural network (TNN) that adaptively determines 3D finite-difference nodalization based on thermal loads and initial conditions, enabling more accurate coarse-mesh calculations. A differentiable finite-difference thermal simulator is embedded within the framework to enforce physical consistency and support efficient training, while an upscaling layer reconstructs high-resolution temperature fields from the coarse-grid solution. The proposed PIML approach is evaluated against high-fidelity fine-mesh simulations, low-fidelity fixed coarse-mesh models, and a purely data-driven artificial neural network (ANN). Results show that the PIML framework improves prediction accuracy by 50% and 39% relative to the coarse-mesh physics model and ANN model, respectively, while maintaining physically consistent thermal distributions. Computationally, the framework is also 3x faster than high-fidelity simulations, demonstrating an effective balance between accuracy and efficiency for thermal modeling of lunar rover systems.

records.title: Firefly Blue Ghost Mission 1: SCALPSS 1.1 Camera Calibration
records.summary: The Stereo Cameras for Lunar Plume-Surface Studies (SCALPSS) payload attached to the Firefly Aerospace Blue Ghost Lander successfully completed its mission in March 2025. This payload was designed to measure the pre- and post-landing lunar surface with six cameras in multiple stereo pair combinations. Two of the cameras focused on the pre-landing surface, while the other four were used to measure the post-landing surface. The difference between these two surfaces was designed to determine the amount of lunar regolith displaced during landing. In order to make these measurements, an extensive calibration procedure was developed. This paper details the intrinsic and extrinsic calibration procedures which were developed for all six cameras to enable triangulation of three-dimensional points on the lunar surface from stereo image pairs.
keywords: Lunar and Planetary Science and Exploration

records.title: Firefly Blue Ghost Mission 1: SCALPSS 1.1 Short Focal Length Camera Descent Imaging
records.summary: Stereoscopic imagery obtained during the Firefly Blue Ghost Mission 1 landing by NASA’s Stereo Cameras for Lunar Plume-Surface Studies (SCALPSS) instrument is reported in this paper. The SCALPSS 1.1 six-camera system operated during transit to the moon, and captured imagery during and after descent to the lunar surface. This paper reports imagery from a pair of cameras equipped with 5.4 mm focal length lenses which imaged the area beneath a pair of reaction control system (RCS) thrusters. Starting at an altitude of 30 m, clear images of the lunar surface were obtained. Around 18 m altitude, clear streaks appear in the images indicating entrainment of lunar dust associated with plume-surface interaction. Closer to landing, additional regolith is lofted, obscuring the images while also visualizing various fluid mechanical phenomena such as a shock structure and streaking behavior. Below 2 m altitude, a pair of circular plumes associated with the RCS thrusters are clearly seen with streaks emanating outward radially. The image intensity alternates between bright and dark, corresponding to the RCS thrusters pulsing. Finally, at landing, the imagery shows the lander settling to a stable resting position. Qualitative discussion of these phenomena is contained herein while quantitative analysis will be reported elsewhere.

records.title: Fleet-To-Lab: A Transfer Learning Framework For Lunar Rover Slippage Estimation Via Model Fusion
records.summary: Accurate wheel slip estimation is essential for autonomous lunar rover mobility and navigation. Machine Learning models trained on terrestrial data generalize poorly to lunar terrain, and real lunar datasets are scarce due to the limited number of missions and costly data acquisition. We present Fleet-to-Lab, a transfer learning framework that leverages proprioceptive data collected by previously deployed heterogeneous lunar rovers to mitigate the Earth-Moon domain gap in slip estimation for a future deployable unit. We fuse several heterogeneous expert models into a single architecture, using a modest dataset collected after the rover deployment. We propose AcoMerge, a new hybrid swarm-intelligence algorithm that performs model fusion by searching for an optimal combi- nation of expert parameters. Experiments conducted in a high- fidelity physics simulation show balanced accuracy and macro- F1 improvements compared to deep model fusion baselines. AcoMerge exhibits competitive performance with joint training on deep architectures, while achieving higher macro-F1 and balanced accuracy on a smaller model. Overall, our framework shows model fusion as a possible transfer learning alternative for slippage estimation in space robotic missions with limited data.

records.title: From ball to rover: Transformable palm-sized rover SORA-Q for autonomous lunar exploration
records.summary: Robotic technologies are expected to drive substantial advancements in planetary exploration and resource prospecting by performing a variety of tasks in extraterrestrial environments. In particular, miniature robots are ideally suited for integration into spacecraft with strict payload limitations, providing a cost-effective solution. However, the pursuit of autonomous exploration using these miniature robots presents challenges owing to constraints in computational power and battery capacity and reduced locomotion performance owing to their small size. Here, we introduce a two-wheeled centimeter-scale rover, designated Lunar Excursion Vehicle 2 (LEV-2), also known as SORA-Q (named after the Japanese words for space and sphere), which transforms into a wheeled configuration from a compact spherical form, enabling efficient traversal of soft lunar terrains. On 19 January 2024 (universal time coordinated), LEV-2 was deployed from a Japanese lunar lander, Smart Lander for Investigating Moon (SLIM), immediately before its landing on the lunar surface. After a lunar landing, the palm-sized rover accomplished autonomous lunar exploration by navigating around the SLIM lander, capturing images of both the SLIM lander and its environment and transmitting selected images through wireless communication on the lunar surface without reliance on ground-based teleoperation. This study details the system design of LEV-2 and presents the results of its in situ lunar activities, highlighting the efficacy of the proposed technologies necessary for mission implementation. Furthermore, we discuss the technical challenges encountered during the mission, including operational constraints and partial data loss, as well as the lessons learned for future exploration missions using small-scale space robots.

records.title: From Exploration Flight Test-1 to Artemis II--A NASA Langley's Orion Aerosciences Overview
records.summary: The Orion Aerosciences program at NASA Langley has played a central role in advancing the aerodynamic and aeroheating prediction capabilities required for the Orion crew vehicle’s return from deep space. This presentation provides a technical overview of aerosciences contributions spanning Exploration Flight Test-1 (EFT-1), Artemis I, and the ongoing post-flight analysis of Artemis II. EFT-1 provided the first high-energy entry dataset for Orion, enabling critical validation of aerodynamic force and moment predictions, static and dynamic stability characteristics, and aeroheating environments at relevant flight Mach and Reynolds numbers. Flight-derived pressure data were used to refine the Flush Air Data System (FADS) methodology for atmospheric density reconstruction and to improve Best Estimated Trajectory (BET) solutions. The EFT-1 data also offered key insights into heat shield performance, including char layer recession, in-depth thermal response, and material retention behavior under flight conditions, informing updates to both thermal response models and uncertainty quantification practices. Building on EFT-1, Artemis I extended the database to true lunar-return conditions. Observations of heat shield performance, including localized char loss, bondline response, and recession variability, provided an unprecedented opportunity to reassess Thermal Protection System (TPS) and aeroheating modeling assumptions. Aerodynamic reconstruction efforts incorporated improved FADS calibration, enhanced atmospheric modeling, and refined force and moment databases to reduce trajectory and load uncertainties. Aeroheating comparisons between pre-flight predictions and flight data enabled targeted model updates, particularly in transitional flow environments and wake heating regions. For Artemis II, these lessons were systematically incorporated into the pre-flight prediction process. Updates included refined aerodynamic databases anchored to flight-validated corrections, improved density estimation and BET methodologies using enhanced database interpolation algorithm and FADS modeling, and revised aeroheating design environments informed by Artemis I material response observations. By the time of the workshop, Artemis II post-flight analysis will be underway, and preliminary findings will be presented where available, including early comparisons of aerodynamic reconstruction, atmospheric density estimation, and thermal protection system performance relative to updated predictions. Collectively, this body of work is a testament to the dedicated and multidisciplinary team whose sustained efforts have contributed to the program’s success and to the progressive maturation of Orion aerosciences modeling through numerical modeling, ground and flight data assimilation. The integrated advancement of aerodynamics, trajectory reconstruction, FADS-based density estimation, and aeroheating analysis has reduced predictive uncertainty and strengthened confidence for ...

records.title: Geo-Standardizing 3D Modeling of Surface/Subsurface Objects and Related Logical Spaces on Celestial Bodies: Case Studies for Moon and Mars
records.summary: Establishing frameworks for promoting the realization of various activities on celestial bodies sustainably is of great significance for different contexts, such as preserving the scientific evidence and space heritage. Therefore, this research first proposes a conceptual model that covers the different types of features, attributes, and relationships between them to comprehensively delineate the surface/subsurface objects and related logical spaces on celestial bodies. It then implements this conceptual model as a CityJSON extension in such a way that allows for creating the three-dimensional (3D) geodatasets that represent these objects and spaces in a standardized manner. Moreover, the usefulness of this study is demonstrated through creating CityJSON datasets that include 3D models of exemplary surface/subsurface objects from the Moon and Mars, such as a historical landing site and related logical spaces, such as exclusion zones for protecting this site. The results of the current study show that there is a strong potential for forming 3D geodatasets on celestial bodies that can provide a notable foundation for the technical implementation of international agreements and legal frameworks. This work also contributes to the design of planetary spatial data infrastructures (PSDI) by incorporating the third dimension.

records.title: Globally Localizing Lunar Rover in Pixels via Graph Alignment
records.summary: Precise rover localization is a prerequisite for autonomous lunar exploration, yet the absence of Global Navigation Satellite System (GNSS) signals and the cumulative drift of local localization methods severely constrain long-range missions. Cross-view localization provides a promising drift-free global solution by matching rover-view and satellite-view imagery. However, the lunar environment poses unique challenges for correspondence alignment, including inter-entity entanglement, inter-viewpoint divergence, and simulation-to-real domain shift. To address these challenges, we propose Warped Alignment of Reprojected Graphs (WARG), a framework that leverages unified graph learning and reprojected graph matching for robust cross-view alignment. Pretrained on the synthetic LuSNAR dataset, WARG achieves an average test error of 0.32 m and demonstrates robust zero-shot generalization to the synthetic lunar south pole region with an error of 3.63 m. More importantly, when validated on real-world data from the YuTu-2 rover, WARG achieves a localization error of 1.68 m within a 100 m x 100 m search area, corresponding to nearly one-pixel precision in low-resolution satellite imagery with a spatial resolution of 1.40 m/pixel. Beyond accuracy, WARG is computationally efficient, containing only 1.56M parameters, corresponding to 16.12% of previous lightweight models, and operating at 5.49 Hz on an NVIDIA RTX A6000 GPU, approaching GNSS-level update frequency. Finally, we observe that WARG naturally develops low-level spatial awareness, including semantic segmentation and structural reasoning, through cross-view localization learning, highlighting its potential as a promising paradigm for spatial intelligence with minimal annotation cost. The source code is available at https://github.com/maochen-casia/warg.

records.title: GN&C Modeling, Simulation, and Integration of ANTS
records.summary: This proposal is one piece in the future development path of Autonomous Network of Teleoperated Systems (ANTS), leveraging assets and expertise from Mission and Fault Management, GN&C, and Human Factors. ANTS closes a critical gap in the interoperability of lunar mobile assets, serving as an “air traffic controller” for multiple heterogenous systems. ANTS-type infrastructure will be necessary if there are two or more lunar assets operating in the same area. The long-term goal is to stand up a high-fidelity simulation in Human Factors' lunar lighting and terrain simulation, LEVR (Lunar Environments in Virtual Reality), utilizing GN&C-generated physics-based rover models, to develop, test, and verify Mission and Fault Management’s ANTS capabilities with multiple rovers in a highly realistic lunar environment. Although this proposal focuses on the GN&C component of the technology maturation path, great care has been taken to ensure extensibility and sustainability for future funding efforts. ROS was selected as the common framework to define the interfaces between all three aspects. This proposal seeks to implement these interfaces and complete the GN&C elements, with support from Mission and Fault Management on critical ANTS updates. GN&C will be responsible for the development of physics-based and kinematically-consistent rover models in an industry-standard GN&C development tool, Simulink. Although a current implementation of ANTS exists within Simulink, rover models are simple and used exclusively for debugging purposes rather than physically-realistic simulations, including holonomic motion, electric motor torque and speed limits, and wheel-slippage. GN&C will implement generalized and extensible rover models in a “crawl, walk, run” fashion, starting with a simple unicycle model, followed by differential drive, followed by steering linkage models. These standardized models are representative and extensible to current and future lunar rover concepts and can be tailored to each mission. GN&C and Mission and Fault Management will implement a ROS wrapper around these models to allow the easy portability of models to other assets, including Human Factors’ LEVR. Mission and Fault Management will assess ANTS performance under several rover models. Benefits: The expected outcome of this study is a maturation of the ANTS technology with physics-based rover models, enabling high quality simulations for a variety of mobile lunar assets. Goals: 1. Integrate Robot Operating System (ROS) framework message passing interface, positioning this work to be readily accessible for future development. 2. Further the capability of Autonomous Network of Teleoperated Systems (ANTS) by increasing the number of rovers that can be commanded in simulation. 3. Increase fidelity of current ANTS rover models in Simulink to use physics-based and kinematically-consistent ...

records.title: Grouping Flight Microphone Sensors as a Phased Array to Determine Noise Sources During Artemis-I Launch
records.summary: NASA’s Artemis vehicle was equipped with many microphones as part of the Development Flight Instrumentations (DFI) during its maiden flight on Nov 16, 2022. While not a part of the flight objectives, it is shown that data from these sensors can be used with beamforming models to determine distribution of noise sources on the Mobile Launcher and on pad 39B during lift-off. The group of DFI sensors created a tall and narrow phased array that moved with the vehicle. Despite a large number of challenges associated with the non-optimal shape, low sampling rate of the time series data, uncertainty in sound-speed estimates, and diffraction around service tower and the vehicle shape, use of the functional beamforming method was found to provide good maps of sound source distribution in the frequency range of 20Hz ≤ f ≤ 100Hz and during the early part of liftoff from t=0s to t=6s duration. The primary noise sources were found to be the northern edge of the Mobile Launcher (ML) and the base of the Service Tower. During early part of the launch, the north trench through which all of the plume and steam mixture were ejected were found also to be the sources of noise for f <30Hz. The higher frequency sounds were found to be around the hole on ML and the base of the Service tower. The latter is a region where plumes from the boosters and the core engines impinged on the ground surface, particularly with increased elevation of Artemis above the pad. Work is in progress to include the effect of Doppler shift in the beamforming scheme. Any improvement from this effort will be included in the final manuscript.

records.title: High-Precision Landing Using Visual-Inertial Odometry
records.summary: I propose an autonomous navigation algorithm that efficiently and accurately estimates spacecraft motion during descent and landing. Future NASA missions require access to scientifically valuable but hazardous sites on the moon and beyond. In these scenarios, the spacecraft must precisely estimate its position and orientation without exceeding the processing limits of its onboard computer. In practice, visual-inertial odometry is useful to navigate uncertain environments, often forming a solution based on data from an onboard camera and inertial measurement unit. I identify multiple sources of estimation error in current approaches, including the misrepresentation of complex dynamics and suboptimal image processing. Through the combined strength of several mathematical tools, I will leverage the inherent characteristics of visual-inertial data to increase estimation accuracy at a low computational cost. Rather than estimate the solution incrementally, all available measurements will be solved together in a factor-graph-based framework, producing a robust understanding of the spacecraft's flight path. By fitting a smooth trajectory that enforces global--not just local--dynamics, I will incorporate high-fidelity motion models between discrete camera images, minimizing error accumulation and decreasing solution drift when integrating spacecraft dynamics. Instead of flat-space coordinates, the algorithm will use geometrically-attractive mathematics to closely capture complex motion. For each image, optimal downselection will dedicate processing power to the most informative measurements. The algorithm will be validated using NASA's Perseverance mission data and an unmanned aerial vehicle experiment, where hardware-in-the-loop efficacy will be tested on a lightweight processor in lunar-like conditions. The proposed algorithm will leverage visual-inertial odometry to enable high-accuracy autonomous navigation in stringent spacecraft landing scenarios. I will jointly utilize robust sensor fusion, globally-enforced integration, naturally nonlinear coordinates, and optimal measurement downselection to achieve accurate, real-time state estimation on a resource-constrained spacecraft. This framework is expected to outperform current software, improving safe landing for future missions.

records.title: High-Speed Observations of Lunar Impact Flashes
records.summary: Lunar impact flashes provide a direct means of estimating the flux of centimetre-sized meteoroids impacting the lunar surface. However, 25-60 frames per second imaging typical of most monitoring programs limit the ability to resolve the rapid temporal evolution of the impact process, while the integration of Earthshine background restricts the detection of faint flashes. In this work, we present high-speed observations of lunar impact flashes captured at 200 and 250 FPS using the Zadko Telescope in Western Australia. We resolve the light curves of four confirmed events, revealing complex morphologies, some of which are not well modelled by simple exponential decays. One event was simultaneously detected by a second observer using a 50 FPS system, revealing a significantly faster brightness drop in the high-speed data that cannot be explained by spectral differences alone, indicating temporal integration of the vapour plume and subsequent ejecta. Our data also indicates that the initial flash intensity (representing the vapour plume) exhibits significantly less variance across events than the total luminous energy. Furthermore, we found no statistical correlation between the initial luminous energy and the total integrated energy of the flashes in this data, suggesting that the physical mechanism driving the initial vapour expansion may be physically decoupled from the longer-duration glow driven by the cooling ejecta. High temporal resolution combined with high sensitivity are therefore essential for accurately characterising the physical properties of the impactor and distinguishing the initial vapour plume from the subsequent incandescent cooling phase, although a significantly larger dataset is required to definitively constrain these mechanisms.

records.title: Human Sensorimotor Limitations for Lunar Rover Driving
records.summary: Artemis crews controlling lunar rovers will face not only the standard neural limitations of human sensorimotor performance, but also multiple and severe challenges unique to spaceflight and to the impoverished lighting condition at the lunar south pole. Though a review of earth-based laboratory, simulator, and real-world measurements, we estimate the following reaction times for crew braking during a lunar rover traverse: For response to an automated audio-warning system (informs auditory alert design/delivery) - Total Human Response Time + Confidence Interval (CI) is expected to be up to 1.6 s. For response by human visual-scan/vigilance (informs Con-Ops and vehicle design) - Total Human Response Time + CI + margin is expected to be up to 3.5 s (to be confirmed by high-fidelity HITL simulator testing).

records.title: Integrated Lander-Propulsion-GNC Framework for Autonomous Lunar Powered Descent
records.summary: This paper presents an integrated lander-propulsion-GNC framework for autonomous lunar powered descent. The BUG VTVL test vehicle serves as the reference platform, with the YUNT V0 throttleable bipropellant engine providing variable thrust across a wide operating envelope, integrated with a real-time successive convexification guidance solver. The vehicle design accounts for structural configuration, landing stability, center-of-mass migration, and inertia evolution, while the propulsion architecture defines the throttle ratio, dead-zone behavior, and gimbal authority that constrain the guidance problem. A successive convexification algorithm addresses all nonconvexities; thrust lower bounds, mass depletion coupling, and thruster dead-zone behavior are all handled within a unified second-order cone program solvable in near-real time. Parametric analysis reveals a fundamental coupling between throttle ratio, pointing authority, and surface gravity. Monte Carlo simulations validate guidance robustness, achieving sub-50-meter landing precision under realistic perturbations.

records.title: JOEEE: Jumping Orientable Extreme Environment Explorer
records.summary: We propose modifying and augmenting the JOEEE hopping and cartwheeling mobility system with a multi-function tether to enable mobility into and long duration operations within a Lunar PSR. The Jumping Orientable Extreme Environment Explorer (JOEEE) is a novel surface mobility platform that enables mission concepts such as exploring craters, Lunar PSRs, Lunar lava tubes, extreme low gravity bodies (comets and asteroids), and interaction with astronauts (is safe to handle). The unique maneuvering capability provided by internal brake-able flywheels in JOEEE facilitates mobility of imagers, spectrometers, magnetometers, and other instruments over and into terrain inaccessible to wheeled/tracked rovers or rocket propelled hoppers while the low cost/complexity of the system enables single or multi-robot mission concepts. The goals of this follow on Early Stage Innovation project are to mature TRL of JOEEE from numerical simulation to laboratory demonstrations, perform life testing of critical mechanisms, and continue to meet with instrument developers to target PRISM, CLPS, Ignition, Artemis, and DALI. Benefits: Modification of JOEEE hopping/cartwheeling mobility system with multi-function tether for Lunar PSR entry and long-duration operations; maturation from numerical simulation to laboratory demonstrations; life testing of critical mechanisms; single and multi-robot mission concept enablement.

records.title: Joint Estimation of Properties of the Lunar Subsurface and Galactic Foregrounds with LuSEE-Night
records.summary: The Lunar Surface Electromagnetics Experiment (LuSEE-Night) is a joint NASA-DOE-ESA low-frequency radio telescope that will reach the lunar far side in 2027. The unknown dielectric properties of the subsurface at the LuSEE-Night landing site impose the most significant limitation for precision instrument calibration, as reflections from the lunar subsurface can change the primary beam at the 10-20% level. Simulations of these effects have provided insight and concern, showing that the lunar subsurface modeled as a lossy dielectric can absorb a large amount of the power of the sky signal. While this absorption may not strongly impact the signal-to-noise ratio in a sky-noise-dominated regime, it could complicate the beam pattern and make the signal more difficult to model and interpret. We have simulated the far-field properties of the LuSEE-Night beam for varying dielectric profiles of the lunar subsurface. We find that varying the properties of the lunar subsurface has the most significant impact around the antenna resonance, impacting its amplitude, position and width. Conversely, changing the properties of the foreground impacts the data across the band. We use a Bayesian inference pipeline to jointly estimate parameters of a galactic foreground model and dielectric properties of the lunar subsurface around the LuSEE-Night landing site and find that parameters of both the galaxy and subsurface properties can be estimated jointly. While the modeling is somewhat idealized, we believe that the results are largely robust owing to the fact that spectral variations for plausible subsurface and galaxy models have very different spectral signatures.

records.title: Local Lyapunov Exponent-Guided Stochastic Midcourse Correction Design of Low-Energy Earth-Moon Transfers
records.summary: Midcourse correction is essential for reliable cislunar transfer missions. For low-energy Earth-Moon transfers, strongly nonuniform error growth makes conventional correction strategies less effective. This paper proposes a stochastic midcourse correction design for low-energy Earth-Moon transfers based on local Lyapunov exponent (LLE). The local error-amplification characteristics of the nominal trajectory are first analyzed using an instantaneous LLE. The analysis shows that strong sensitivity is concentrated near periapsis, and that the LLE maxima coincide with regions of strong finite-time error growth. These maxima are therefore used to segment the trajectory and define the number of corrections. Based on this segmentation, a reduced parameterization is introduced to describe the correction epochs, while second-order state transition tensors (STTs) are employed for nonlinear correction targeting. The resulting timing variables are then optimized through a sample-average approximation of the chance-constrained stochastic problem. Paired Monte Carlo simulations show that, under the same mission-accuracy requirements, the proposed strategy greatly improves the reliability and robustness of trajectory recovery while requiring less correction cost than the classical Breakwell spacing-ratio strategy.

records.title: Low-Energy and Low-Thrust Exploration Tour of Saturnian Moons with Full Lunar Surface Coverage
records.summary: This study presents the trajectory design for a mission touring Saturn's Inner Large Moons (Rhea, Dione, Tethys, Enceladus, and Mimas) engineered to meet observational requirements, including full surface coverage, while ensuring low fuel consumption and compatibility with current power and propulsion technologies (radioisotope thermoelectric generators and Hall effect thrusters). The tour begins at Rhea and ends at Mimas, using a trajectory concept that alternates between extended observation phases around each moon and Saturn centered low-thrust spiral arcs to transition efficiently to the next target. The J2-perturbed Circular Restricted Three-Body Problem is adopted to design exploration paths, with halo orbits serving as staging points for heteroclinic and homoclinic loops that enable prolonged, repeated, and comprehensive surface reconnaissance (including critical regions such as Enceladus poles, where geological activity produces intense plumes). Stable and unstable hyperbolic invariant manifolds of the halo orbits act as departure and arrival gateways for propelled inter-moon transfers, modeled in an ephemeris-based framework including gravitational perturbations from the moons, the Sun, and Saturn's oblateness. The dynamical model setup is guided by a rigorous perturbation analysis to maximize computational efficiency while maintaining high fidelity trajectory design. A locally optimal guidance law minimizes propellant consumption. The proposed tour offers an alternative to traditional flyby missions, providing comparable total duration but greater observing time and reduced fuel requirements, and advances previous work by achieving both complete lunar surface coverage and high-fidelity modeling.

records.title: Lunar Lander Landing Dynamic Model and App Development in Simscape
records.summary: With the recent renewed interest in manned Lunar exploration, it is critical to revisit the Apollo Moon landings with new analysis tools. Modeling the Moon landings of the past can help guide the development of new landing vehicles for the present and the future. One of the critical subsystems to model is the vehicle’s landing gear. During a landing event, structural loading, energy absorption, and toppling stability are important factors that drive the design of landing gear subsystems. These aspects can be studied using models and simulations in addition to physical testing. This study explores one recent modeling tool for modeling the landing gear and uses the Apollo 11 Moon landing as a use case. A generic model was built using MATLAB®, Simulink®, and Simscape® Multibody to model the dynamics of a landing event. The landing gear structure comprising the primary strut, secondary struts, footpads, and joints were modeled in Simscape® Multibody. Various energy absorption mechanisms in the struts were modeled based on the relative motions of the inner and outer cylinders of the leg. Touchdown contact forces, when the footpads strike the lunar surface, were modeled considering the soil mechanical properties. Slosh dynamics were modeled using a mechanical pendulum module and tip-over controllers were developed using Simulink®. However, neither were applied in the presented analysis relating to the Apollo lunar module. After developing the generic landing dynamic model, the Apollo 11 landing was simulated for validation purposes with results closely matching the historical measured data. A MATLAB® Graphical User Interface application (app) also was developed based on this model for usability and better accessibility of the landing simulation by non-experts on landing dynamics. It offered the opportunity for landing stability study with and without control, i.e., the max slope a lander can land without tipping over in 3D realistic landing situations.
keywords: Lunar and Planetary Science and Exploration

records.title: Lunar Rover Cargo Transport: Mission Concept and Field Test
records.summary: In future operations on the lunar surface, automated vehicles will be required to transport cargo between known locations. Such vehicles must be able to navigate precisely in safe regions to avoid natural hazards, human-constructed infrastructure, and dangerous dark shadows. Rovers must be able to park their cargo autonomously within a small tolerance to achieve a successful pickup and delivery. In this field test, Lidar Teach and Repeat provides an ideal autonomy solution for transporting cargo in this way. A one-tonne path-to-flight rover was driven in a semi-autonomous remote-control mode to create a network of safe paths. Once the route was taught, the rover immediately repeated the entire network of paths autonomously while carrying cargo. The closed-loop performance is accurate enough to align the vehicle to the cargo and pick it up. This field report describes a two-week deployment at the Canadian Space Agency's Analogue Terrain, culminating in a simulated lunar operation to evaluate the system's capabilities. Successful cargo collection and delivery were demonstrated in harsh environmental conditions.

records.title: Lunar Surface Science Workshop (LSSW) Landing Site Workshop For Artemis IV: Final Report
records.summary: This authoritative report represents the workshop’s primary deliverable to synthesize community input into candidate FOMs, which NASA can leverage during the Artemis IV landing site evaluation and prioritization process to maximize the scientific return. This work is a useful step towards applying the scientific community’s expertise to help optimize science-related outcomes for the Artemis IV mission.
keywords: Lunar and Planetary Science and Exploration

records.title: LunarRF: A Terrain-Aware Propagation Engine and Pole-Wide 3GPP Surface Coverage Atlas of the Lunar South Pole
records.summary: Artemis surface operations will depend on 3GPP cellular links, yet no public product shows where such links are physically possible across the lunar south pole. We present LunarRF, a GPU system for terrain-aware surface coverage, and the pole-wide atlas produced with it. A footprint engine casts 8192 radial profiles from one of 11,827 candidate masts enumerated by stated rules on the orbit-adjusted LOLA elevation model, takes the viewshed, and evaluates ITU-R P.1812 Delta-Bullington propagation on every profile, continuous through the radio horizon. An order-independent resolver merges the footprints per 20 m cell, making the run shardable and resumable. The atlas covers the disc south of 80°S at 20 m for four SFCG-recommended surface bands and the IM-2 demonstration band, 1.8 to 25.375 GHz, under a stated link budget, storing per cell the best-server power and identity, redundancy count, line of sight and coverability. The engine is validated against a parabolic-equation solver, ray tracing and analytic solutions. Swapping Deygout for Delta-Bullington, or adding terrain noise at the level of the published height-error map of the DEM, moves the coverable class on under 1% of a mast's disc in the mean. With every candidate active, 90.5% of the disc is coverable at 1.8 GHz, 59% at 5.855 GHz and 10% at 25.375 GHz, or 84, 43 and 5% after the measured 3-4 dB engine optimism. A mast covers about 90% of its visible area within its budget-set range, and no band is terrain-limited. The nine current Artemis regions are 85-99% coverable at 1.8 GHz and 22-85% at 5.855 GHz. The atlas and candidate table are released with a DOI.

records.title: MARE: An Open-Source Lunar Rover Simulator with Shadow Ground Truth for Perception and Autonomy
records.summary: Lunar surface exploration increasingly relies on autonomous rovers that must perceive and traverse unstructured terrain under extreme illumination conditions. Near the lunar poles, low sun elevations produce long, high-contrast shadows that challenge stereo vision, terrain segmentation, and localization. Developing perception and navigation algorithms for these conditions requires large amounts of sensor data with accurate ground truth, which field campaigns and analog facilities can only provide at high cost and with limited variety. This paper presents MARE (Modular Autonomy and Rendering Environment), an open-source simulation suite for lunar rover perception and autonomy built on Unreal Engine 5 and ROS 2. MARE consists of three integrated components. Terrain Studio generates cratered and rocky lunar Digital Elevation Maps (DEMs) to build simulation scenes. A dedicated Unreal Engine project hosts two physics-based rovers with plugins for stereo, lidar, event, and Single-Photon Avalanche Diode (SPAD) cameras, streaming time-stamped sensor data and pixel-accurate ground truth. Lastly, a Guidance, Navigation, and Control (GNC) stack provides web-based mission control. Validation shows a mean Intersection over Union (IoU) of 0.79 between predicted and rendered shadows at low sun elevations, and stereo depth analysis verifies decreased pixel coverage in shadowed regions relative to sunlit terrain.

records.title: Mitigating plume surface interactions using lunar craters
records.summary: Launching and landing spacecraft on the lunar surface mobilizes regolith at high velocities which will likely cause damage to nearby objects and infrastructure, a phenomenon known as plume surface interactions (PSIs) that must be mitigated for sustainable lunar surface exploration. While some mitigation strategies prescribe the construction of walls and landing pads using locally sourced regolith and additive manufacturing techniques, cheaper and more immediately available approaches may be required. We introduce a novel concept that uses small lunar craters (<1.5 km) as unprepared landing sites to mitigate the hazards posed by PSIs. We simulated the ballistic trajectories of regolith grains ejected by PSIs from the centers of 238 lunar craters and find that many could completely shield nearby areas from ejected regolith, with some of these protected "umbrella zones" being large enough to host either a 16 m-tall Blue Moon Mk. 2 lander or a lunar outpost. These examined craters are also conducive to safe landings as they retain sufficiently large and flat crater floors, as well as crater walls that are traversable by the Artemis program's proposed Lunar Terrain Vehicle. However, much work remains for this approach to be fully relied upon as a mitigation strategy.

records.title: Modeling resonance characteristics of the Chang'e-7 lander modulated by solar panel rotation under lunar south-pole thermal environment
records.summary: The Chang'e-7 (CE-7) mission will deploy the first seismometer at the lunar south pole to detect moonquakes and probe lunar interior structures in 2026 winter. However, the lander's vibration response to the extreme temperature cycles of the polar environment remains unclear, complicating the analysis of noise sources in seismic records. Here, we developed a high-fidelity finite-element model of the CE-7 lander to characterize its resonant behavior under the coupled influence of solar panel rotation and extreme thermal variations. Numerical results reveal that the lander's fundamental frequency (~0.76 Hz) at room temperature drifts significantly between 0.64 Hz and 0.87 Hz when the outside temperature varies from -180 to +80 °C. This frequency drift is primarily driven by thermally induced stiffness changes in the solar array supporting bracket, whereas geometric reconfiguration due to rotation plays a secondary role. Crucially, this resonance band directly overlaps with the primary seismic observation window (usually <1.0 Hz). Sensitivity analysis further confirms that the fundamental mode remains structurally robust despite material property uncertainties. These findings establish an essential theoretical baseline for identifying and filtering lander-induced resonant noise, which will be immediately applicable upon the acquisition of the first in-situ seismic datasets from the south pole of the Moon, ensuring the high fidelity of accurate lunar interior detection.

records.title: MOON: Multi-Objective OrthoNormalized Updates for Multitask Learning
records.summary: Multi-objective optimization (MOO) has demonstrated significant success in multi-task learning by mitigating task conflicts through gradient manipulation. However, most existing methods flatten model parameters into vectors and perform gradient manipulation under Euclidean geometry, thereby overlooking the matrix structure prevalent in modern architectures such as Transformers. In this paper, we show that gradient manipulation in Euclidean space does not generally yield the steepest descent direction under matrix geometry, potentially limiting optimization efficiency. Drawing from the theory of steepest descent for matrix-valued parameters, we propose MOON (Multi-Objective OrthoNormalized Updates), which performs gradient manipulation under spectral--nuclear norm geometry and uses the orthonormalized manipulated gradient for parameter updates. Theoretically, for smooth non-convex objectives, we establish convergence of the averaged Pareto-stationarity measure at rates of $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/2})$ in the deterministic setting and $\mathcal{O}(T^{-1/4})$ under stochastic gradients. Empirical results across various benchmarks show that MOON consistently improves both optimization efficiency and final multi-task performance. Our code is available at https://github.com/KunlinLyu/MOON.

records.title: NASA Plume-Surface Interaction (PSI) Testing to Reduce Risk from Propulsive Landing
records.summary: NASA's Artemis program will return humans to the surface of the Moon for the first time since the final Apollo mission in December 1972. The new lunar landers are larger, more powerful, and utilize different concepts of operations from those flown during the Apollo era. During descent and landing, the environment resulting from the impingement of rocket engine exhaust onto regolith, or plume-surface interactions (PSI), poses a potential hazard to all propulsive landing vehicles, as well as nearby assets and payloads supporting exploration of the surface. Understanding these phenomena has challenged lander design since the 1960s, and new test data are required to enable NASA’s lunar exploration goals and to safely fly these new vehicles. At present, NASA is conducting ground testing in a vacuum sphere to obtain data relevant for prediction of the PSI environments produced by human-scale landing systems. This presentation will discuss the test objectives, design, execution, challenges, and data products.

records.title: NASA Space Launch System Artemis I & II Post Flight Ascent Aerothermal Environments Overview
records.summary: Since 2011 the Aerosciences Branch/EV33 at NASA Marshall Space Flight Center has been involved with the development of ascent external aerothermal environments for the NASA Space Launch System (SLS) Block 1 launch vehicle for the purposes of supporting thermal analysis and the design of thermal protection systems. The SLS Block 1 Artemis I and II launch vehicles successfully launched from Pad39B at NASA Kennedy Space Center on November 16th, 2022 and April 1st, 2026, respectively. Over 70 aerothermal islands, consisting of over 265 operational instruments captured aerodynamic heating and plume induced environments throughout the launch vehicles. Gauges consisted of calorimeters, radiometers, gas temperature probes, pressure transducers, bi-directional pressure probes and thermocouples. Prior to launch, aerothermal design environment models were generated to predict ascent aerodynamic heating and plume induced environments over a design space that covered a range of vehicle trajectories that varied atmospheric, vehicle performance, and off-nominal, engine-out conditions. Post flight reconstruction models were developed for each flight island using the Day-of-Launch (DOL) Best Equivalent Trajectory (BET) that provided freestream conditions and propulsion system boundary conditions. This paper discusses a summary of the ascent aerothermal environments observed during the flights and the respective modelling approaches and the performance of them through comparisons of flight data and predictions.

records.title: NASA’S Human Landing System: Demonstrating the Capability to Land Artemis Astronauts on the Moon by 2028
records.summary: NASA’s Human Landing System (HLS) program, managed out of Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Ala., is working with United States industry to develop and demonstrate the capability to land crew and large cargo on the Moon in support of the U. S. Administration’s goal of landing astronauts on the Moon by 2028. The HLS program is working with SpaceX to develop a variant of its Starship as an HLS and with Blue Origin to develop its Blue Moon MK2 to serve as an HLS for a series of increasingly challenging Artemis missions. The HLS program is making progress toward the first crewed lunar landing of the Artemis program by performing risk reduction and testing activities where needed, such as carrying out the largest ground-based study of plume-surface interaction (PSI) in history. A particularly impactful aspect of the program is making NASA engineers, subject matter experts (SMEs), and facilities available to SpaceX and Blue Origin through collaborations and Government Task Agreements (GTAs). Both companies have taken advantage of collaborations with NASA experts and GTAs at specialized facilities at nearly every NASA center. These public-private partnerships are advancing technology readiness and reducing risks in key areas, such as cryogenic valve development, cryogenic fluid management (CFM), computational fluid dynamics (CFD), wind tunnel testing, vibrational testing of avionics and other electronic equipment, thermal testing and modeling of various materials, and more. Both SpaceX and Blue Origin have made significant progress on lander development for both crew and large cargo during the past year. This paper will review progress the HLS program and its commercial providers have made during the past year and look ahead to significant developments leading up to the first Artemis missions using the human landing systems currently under development.
keywords: Lunar and Planetary Science and Exploration

records.title: NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) Rocket Ready for Artemis II Lunar Mission
records.summary: In early 2026, NASA will launch the Artemis II mission, an approximately 10-day long lunar mission that will fly three NASA astronauts and one CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut on a free-return trajectory around the Moon, following a one-day checkout of their Orion spacecraft in Earth orbit. The mission will be the first to launch astronauts aboard NASA’s Orion spacecraft and on top of the agency’s SLS (Space Launch System) rocket. The mission will also deploy four 12U CubeSats as secondary payloads from the Orion stage adapter, following Orion separation and departure. The payloads, developed by four of NASA’s international partners, will perform a variety of science and technology investigations. The SLS and Orion for the mission are currently stacked in the Vehicle Assembly Building (VAB) at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center in Florida and are undergoing final preparations to rollout to Launch Pad 39B for a tanking test before launch. In addition to preparations for the Artemis II mission, significant progress is being made on the SLS for the Artemis III mission, which is targeted to return astronauts to the lunar surface no later than 2029. Major components of the core stage and solid rocket boosters are already at NASA Kennedy undergoing build-up for the mission. Data from the Artemis II launch and mission, as well as progress to subsequent missions, as available, will be presented.

records.title: NASA’s SLS (Space Launch System) Super Heavy-Lift Rocket in Process for Artemis II and Beyond
records.summary: NASA is preparing the SLS (Space Launch System) rocket for the Artemis II mission, which will launch the first crew to the Moon since 1972. The mission, launching no later than April 2026, will send four astronauts on a ten-day mission to the Moon and back, using a free-return trajectory. Four of the major elements of the SLS for Artemis II are at NASA’s Kennedy Space Center or at United Launch Alliance’s Cape Canaveral Space Force Station facilities in Florida. The final element of SLS, the Orion stage adapter, will arrive at Kennedy in 2025. Vehicle integration is underway with stacking the two solid rocket boosters on the mobile launcher, and the core stage being placed in a new vertical workstation in High Bay 2 in the Vehicle Assembly Building at Kennedy, undergoing final preparations for stacking. The flight software is loaded on the flight computers. Hardware for Artemis III, IV, and V is in various stages of production and processing at NASA and contractor facilities across the country. Test articles for the exploration upper stage, universal stage adapter, and payload adapter that will fly on the SLS Block 1B variant are in testing at NASA’s Marshall Space Flight Center in Huntsville, Alabama. Block 1B will debut on Artemis IV. Its flight software is also in development. In 2024, NASA and L3Harris Technologies completed the certification test program of the new production RS-25 liquid engines that power the core stage. Acceptance hot fire of the first new production engine is expected in spring 2025. Development of the evolved solid rocket boosters that will debut on Artemis IX will feature a full-scale test in 2025. Hardware progress for multiple Artemis missions and the capabilities of SLS to support the nation’s most ambitious missions will be presented.
